Animal Farm by George Orwell

3 chapter chunks · character map · theme analysis · final test · hand-drawn cartoon project

📖 Welcome to Animal Farm

SOL 9.RL · ~25 min

Animal Farm is a short novel by George Orwell, published in 1945. It's only about 100 pages — but it is one of the most famous books in English.

It looks like a story about farm animals who chase the farmer away and try to run the farm themselves. But it is really about something bigger.

📕
Read the Book (PDF)
Full text of Animal Farm — about 100 pages. Read it before each chapter quiz.
📖 Open PDF →
What is it really about? Orwell wrote Animal Farm to describe the Russian Revolution of 1917. The animals = the Russian people. The pigs = the leaders (especially Stalin). It is an allegory — a story where the characters secretly stand for real people or ideas.

The setting

The whole story takes place on Manor Farm in England, owned by the cruel and drunk farmer Mr. Jones. The animals work hard, are not well-fed, and are killed when they get old.

Who are the main characters?

Old Major
Wise old boar
Gives the first speech that starts the rebellion. Dies before it happens. (Based on Karl Marx / Lenin.)
Napoleon
Pig · main villain
A clever, ruthless pig. Takes over the farm and becomes a dictator. (Based on Joseph Stalin.)
Snowball
Pig · rival
Smart, idealistic. Wants to make life better. Napoleon chases him away. (Based on Leon Trotsky.)
Squealer
Pig · propaganda
A great talker who twists words so the pigs always look good. (Based on Soviet propaganda media.)
Boxer
Cart-horse · hero worker
Strong, loyal, hard-working. His motto: "I will work harder." He represents the working class.
Clover
Mare · kind worker
A motherly horse. She senses something is wrong but cannot read well enough to be sure.
Benjamin
Old donkey · skeptic
The smartest animal. He sees what is really happening but stays silent. He says: "Donkeys live a long time."
Mr. Jones
Human farmer
The cruel owner of the farm. (Based on Tsar Nicholas II of Russia.)
Mollie
Vain mare
A pretty horse who only cares about ribbons and sugar. Leaves the farm early.
Moses
Tame raven
Tells stories about "Sugarcandy Mountain" (heaven). Represents the church.
The Dogs
Napoleon's secret police
9 dogs Napoleon raises in secret. He uses them to scare and kill anyone who disagrees.
The Sheep
Mindless followers
They chant slogans like "Four legs good, two legs bad." They cannot think for themselves.

🐖 Chapters 1–3 — Old Major's Dream & the Rebellion

~45 min reading + study guide

📖 Open Animal Farm PDF

Chapter 1 summary

One night, the old boar named Old Major calls all the animals into the barn. He has had a dream. He tells them: "Man is the only real enemy we have." Humans take everything the animals produce and give nothing back.

He teaches them a song called "Beasts of England" — a song about a future world where animals are free. Then he dies a few days later.

Chapter 2 summary

The other pigs — Napoleon, Snowball, and Squealer — turn Old Major's ideas into a system called Animalism.

One night, Mr. Jones forgets to feed the animals. They break into the food store. He tries to whip them — and the animals turn on him and chase him off the farm! The rebellion has happened.

The animals rename the farm Animal Farm and paint the Seven Commandments on the barn wall:

  1. Whatever goes upon two legs is an enemy.
  2. Whatever goes upon four legs, or has wings, is a friend.
  3. No animal shall wear clothes.
  4. No animal shall sleep in a bed.
  5. No animal shall drink alcohol.
  6. No animal shall kill any other animal.
  7. All animals are equal.

Chapter 3 summary

The animals harvest the hay — and it is the best harvest the farm has ever had. They work together. Everyone is happy.

The pigs do not do physical labor — they "supervise." Boxer the horse takes the motto "I will work harder."

The pigs secretly take the milk and apples for themselves. Squealer explains: pigs need them to "think." If the pigs cannot think, Mr. Jones will come back!

Watch for this: The pigs are already taking more than other animals — and Squealer is already lying to make it sound okay. This is the first crack in the dream.

Study Guide Questions (Chapters 1–3)

0

⚔️ Chapters 4–7 — The Battle, the Windmill, & the Purge

~50 min reading + study guide

📖 Open Animal Farm PDF

Chapter 4 summary

News of the rebellion spreads. The neighboring farmers (Mr. Pilkington and Mr. Frederick) get scared. Mr. Jones and other men come back with guns to take the farm back.

The animals fight bravely. Snowball plans the battle. The men are driven away. The animals call it the Battle of the Cowshed and create medals for heroes.

Chapter 5 summary

Snowball wants to build a windmill — it will make life easier for everyone. Napoleon disagrees.

At the big meeting, Napoleon suddenly calls his secret dogs. They chase Snowball off the farm forever. Snowball is gone.

Napoleon announces: there will be no more meetings. The pigs will make all the decisions. Then he says: actually, the windmill is a great idea — it was Napoleon's idea all along.

Big lie: Squealer convinces the animals that Snowball was a traitor working with Mr. Jones the whole time. The animals don't remember it that way — but Squealer says they're confused.

Chapter 6 summary

The animals work like slaves to build the windmill. Boxer works hardest. New motto added: "Napoleon is always right."

Napoleon starts trading with humans (which the Commandments forbid). Squealer says the Commandments don't say anything about trade. The animals are not sure — but they don't argue.

A storm knocks the windmill down. Napoleon blames Snowball. He says Snowball is sneaking onto the farm at night to ruin everything.

Chapter 7 summary

This is the saddest chapter so far. The animals are starving. The hens are forced to give up their eggs. They protest. Napoleon starves them until 9 hens die.

Napoleon calls a meeting. He accuses many animals of working with Snowball. The dogs kill them on the spot. Many animals confess to things they didn't do, just to make it stop.

The Commandment that says "No animal shall kill any other animal" has been broken. The animals look at the barn wall. The Commandment now reads:

  1. No animal shall kill any other animal without cause.

They don't remember "without cause" being there before — but maybe they were wrong.

Study Guide Questions (Chapters 4–7)

0

🐷 Chapters 8–10 — Boxer's End & the Final Betrayal

~50 min reading + study guide

📖 Open Animal Farm PDF

Chapter 8 summary

Mr. Frederick (a neighbor) attacks the farm with men carrying guns. They blow up the windmill the animals just rebuilt. The animals win the Battle of the Windmill — but they pay a high price. Boxer is wounded.

The pigs find whiskey in the farmhouse. Napoleon drinks it. Late at night, Squealer is caught at the bottom of a ladder by the barn wall, with a paintbrush. The next morning, the Commandment reads:

  1. No animal shall drink alcohol to excess.

Chapter 9 summary

Winter is hard. Food is short. Rations are cut — but Squealer calls it a "readjustment," not a cut.

Boxer is getting old and weaker. He gets hurt while pulling stones for the windmill. The pigs promise to send him to a hospital.

A truck comes to take him away. As it drives off, Benjamin (the smart old donkey) reads the side of the truck out loud: "Alfred Simmonds, Horse Slaughterer and Glue Boiler". Boxer is being taken to be killed!

The animals chase the truck. But Boxer is too weak to kick the doors open. He is gone.

A few days later, Squealer says Boxer died peacefully in the hospital — and the truck saying "slaughterer" was just an old truck the vet had bought. The animals believe him.

This is the breaking point: Boxer worked his whole life for the farm. The pigs sold him for whiskey money.

Chapter 10 summary

Years pass. The farm has more machines and is richer. But the animals are still hungry. Only the pigs and dogs live well.

One day, the animals see something amazing: the pigs are walking on TWO LEGS. They are carrying whips. The sheep, well-trained by Squealer, chant a new slogan: "Four legs good, TWO legs BETTER!"

The animals run to the barn. All Seven Commandments are gone. In their place is one sentence:

ALL ANIMALS ARE EQUAL
BUT SOME ANIMALS ARE MORE EQUAL THAN OTHERS

The final scene

The pigs invite human farmers over for dinner. The animals look in the window. They see the pigs eating, drinking, and playing cards with the men.

Suddenly there is a loud argument over cards. The animals look from pig to man, and man to pig — and they realize they cannot tell the difference anymore.

The story ends. The revolution has come full circle. The pigs have become exactly what they fought against.

🎭 The 5 Big Themes of Animal Farm

SOL 9.RL.1 · Use these for your cartoon project!

Theme 1
Power Corrupts

The pigs started with good ideas. But once they had power, they became cruel — even crueler than Mr. Jones. The book shows that when people have power, it changes them.

Quote: "All animals are equal, but some animals are more equal than others."

Theme 2
Propaganda & Lies

Squealer uses big words and fast talking to make the animals believe lies. He twists the Commandments. He says Snowball was always a traitor. He says Boxer died peacefully.

Quote: "Surely, comrades, you don't want Jones back?" (Squealer's go-to threat.)

Theme 3
Education = Power

The pigs teach themselves to read first. The other animals never really learn. This is why the pigs can change the Commandments — most animals can't read well enough to notice.

If you can't read, you can't fight back when leaders lie to you.

Theme 4
Loyalty Can Be Used Against You

Boxer's loyalty was his strength. But it was also his weakness. He trusted the pigs to the end. He worked himself to death — and they sold his body for whiskey.

Quote: "I will work harder." — Boxer

Theme 5
Revolution Can Be Betrayed

The animals wanted to be free. They got rid of Mr. Jones — but ended up with someone WORSE. By the end, the pigs are walking on two legs and dressing like humans. Nothing changed.

This is Orwell's warning: a revolution can end up with new oppressors who look just like the old ones.

Algebra I Review

8 short topics · worked examples · 30-question SOL practice test · all self-grading

🔤 Topic 1 — Variables & Expressions

SOL A.EO.1 · ~30 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Foundations

A variable is a letter that stands for a number. Most common: x and y.

An expression is a math phrase like 3x + 5. To evaluate an expression, you plug a number in for the variable.

Example 1

Evaluate 3x + 5 when x = 4.

3(4) + 5 = 12 + 5 = 17
Example 2

Evaluate 2a − b when a = 6 and b = 3.

2(6) − 3 = 12 − 3 = 9

Order of Operations (PEMDAS)

Always do math in this order:

  1. Parentheses
  2. Exponents
  3. Multiply & Divide (left to right)
  4. Add & Subtract (left to right)
Example 3

Evaluate 2 + 3 × 4.

Multiply first: 3 × 4 = 12
Then add: 2 + 12 = 14

⚖️ Topic 2 — Solving Equations

SOL A.EO.4 · ~40 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Solving Equations

To solve an equation means to find the value of x.

Big idea: Whatever you do to one side, do to the other.

One-step equations

Example 4

Solve x + 7 = 12

Subtract 7 from both sides:
x = 12 − 7
x = 5
Example 5

Solve 3x = 21

Divide both sides by 3:
x = 21 ÷ 3
x = 7

Two-step equations

Example 6

Solve 2x + 5 = 13

Step 1: Subtract 5 → 2x = 8
Step 2: Divide by 2 → x = 4
Check your answer: Plug it back in. 2(4) + 5 = 8 + 5 = 13 ✓

📈 Topic 3 — Linear Functions (Slope & y-intercept)

SOL A.F.1 · ~45 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Linear Equations & Graphs

A linear function makes a straight line when you graph it.

Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
  • m = slope (how steep)
  • b = y-intercept (where the line crosses the y-axis)
Example 7

Find the slope and y-intercept of y = 3x + 2.

Slope (m) = 3
y-intercept (b) = 2 → the line crosses the y-axis at (0, 2)

Slope formula

m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)

This is "rise over run." How much y changes ÷ how much x changes.

Example 8

Find the slope between (1, 2) and (4, 8).

m = (8 − 2) / (4 − 1) = 6 / 3 = 2

Special slopes

  • Positive slope (m > 0): line goes UP →
  • Negative slope (m < 0): line goes DOWN →
  • Slope = 0: horizontal line (flat)
  • Undefined slope: vertical line

📋 Topic 4 — Functions, Domain & Range

SOL A.F.1 · ~25 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Functions

A function is a rule: you put in a number, you get out a number. Like a machine.

Notation: f(x) = 2x + 1 means "the function of x is 2x plus 1."

Example 9

If f(x) = 2x + 1, find f(3).

f(3) = 2(3) + 1 = 6 + 1 = 7

Domain & Range

  • Domain = all the x-values you can put IN to the function.
  • Range = all the y-values that come OUT.

Think: Domain = INPUTS. Range = OUTPUTS.

⚡ Topic 5 — Exponent Rules

SOL A.EO.2 · ~30 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Exponents

Exponents tell you how many times to multiply. x³ = x · x · x

Exponent Rules (memorize these!)

Multiply same base: xa · xb = xa+b    (add the exponents)
Divide same base: xa ÷ xb = xa−b    (subtract)
Power of a power: (xa)b = xa·b    (multiply)
Negative exponent: x−a = 1 / xa
Zero exponent: x⁰ = 1    (anything ⁰ = 1)
Example 10

Simplify x² · x⁵.

Same base → add exponents: 2 + 5 = 7
Answer: x⁷
Example 11

Simplify (x³)².

Power of a power → multiply: 3 · 2 = 6
Answer: x⁶

📦 Topic 6 — Polynomials & Factoring

SOL A.EO.3 · ~35 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Polynomials & Factoring

A polynomial is an expression with variables and exponents, like 3x² + 5x − 2.

Adding polynomials

Combine "like terms" (terms with the same variable and exponent).

Example 12

Add (2x² + 3x) + (5x² − x)

Combine x² terms: 2x² + 5x² = 7x²
Combine x terms: 3x + (−x) = 2x
Answer: 7x² + 2x

Multiplying with FOIL

For (x + a)(x + b): First, Outer, Inner, Last.

Example 13

Multiply (x + 3)(x + 4)

F: x · x = x²
O: x · 4 = 4x
I: 3 · x = 3x
L: 3 · 4 = 12
Combine: x² + 7x + 12

Factoring (going backwards)

To factor x² + 7x + 12: find 2 numbers that multiply to 12 and add to 7.

3 and 4! So x² + 7x + 12 = (x + 3)(x + 4)

📊 Topic 7 — Quadratics

SOL A.F.3 · ~25 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Quadratics

A quadratic equation looks like ax² + bx + c = 0. Its graph is a U-shape called a parabola.

Three ways to solve quadratics

  1. Factor (if it factors nicely)
  2. Quadratic formula (always works)
  3. Graph and find where it crosses x-axis

The Quadratic Formula

x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a)

This is on your SOL formula sheet — don't memorize it, just look it up.

Example 14

Solve x² + 5x + 6 = 0 by factoring.

Find 2 numbers that multiply to 6 and add to 5: 2 and 3
So (x + 2)(x + 3) = 0
x = −2 or x = −3

🎯 Topic 8 — Word Problems & Test Tips

~20 min

📺 Watch on Khan Academy → Word Problems

Word problem strategy

  1. Read the problem twice.
  2. Underline the question.
  3. Pick a variable for the unknown (usually x).
  4. Write an equation.
  5. Solve it.
  6. Check — does the answer make sense?
SOL test tips:
  • Use the formula sheet — it's free help.
  • Plug answer choices BACK INTO the question if you get stuck.
  • Skip hard problems and come back.
  • Show your work on scratch paper — don't try to do it all in your head.
  • Answer EVERY question (no penalty for guessing).

📋 Algebra I Formula Sheet

Print this out and have it on the day of the test.

Linear Functions

Slope-intercept form: y = mx + b
Point-slope form: y − y₁ = m(x − x₁)
Standard form: Ax + By = C
Slope: m = (y₂ − y₁) / (x₂ − x₁)

Exponent Rules

xa · xb = xa+b
xa / xb = xa−b
(xa)b = xa·b
x−a = 1 / xa
x⁰ = 1

Quadratics

Standard form: ax² + bx + c = 0
Quadratic formula: x = (−b ± √(b² − 4ac)) / (2a)
Discriminant: b² − 4ac

Geometry (on SOL formula sheet)

Rectangle: P = 2l + 2w · A = lw
Square: P = 4s · A = s²
Triangle: A = ½bh
Pythagorean Thm: a² + b² = c²

Environmental Science

6 readings · 30-term vocab drill · 40-question Final Test · 1 field journal project

🌍 Reading 1 — Earth as a System

SOL ENV.2 · ~25 minutes

Earth is one big system. A system is a group of parts that work together. Earth's parts are:

  • Atmosphere — the air around Earth
  • Hydrosphere — all the water (oceans, rivers, lakes, ice)
  • Geosphere — the rocks and ground
  • Biosphere — all the living things

All four parts depend on each other. A change in one changes the others. For example, when we cut down a forest (biosphere), the air gets warmer (atmosphere) and the soil washes away (geosphere).

Earth gets its energy from the Sun. Plants use sunlight to make their own food. This is called photosynthesis.

Big Idea: Matter cycles through Earth. Energy flows through Earth. Nothing is wasted — water, carbon, and nutrients keep moving around.

🌳 Reading 2 — Ecosystems & Food Chains

SOL ENV.4 · ~30 minutes

An ecosystem is all the living and non-living things in an area. A forest, a pond, a desert — these are ecosystems.

Living vs. Non-living

  • Biotic = living (plants, animals, bacteria, fungi)
  • Abiotic = non-living (sunlight, water, air, soil, temperature)

The 3 jobs in an ecosystem

  • Producers — make their own food using sunlight. (Plants! Algae!)
  • Consumers — eat other living things. (Animals!)
  • Decomposers — break down dead stuff. (Bacteria! Mushrooms! Worms!)

Energy in a food chain

☀️ Sun
→
🌱 Grass (Producer)
→
🐰 Rabbit (Consumer)
→
🦊 Fox (Consumer)
→
🍄 Decomposer

Energy moves up the chain. Each level loses energy (most as heat). That's why there are MANY plants, fewer rabbits, and only a few foxes.

Biodiversity

Biodiversity = the variety of living things in an ecosystem. More biodiversity = a stronger, healthier ecosystem.

When an animal that doesn't belong is introduced, it's called an invasive species. Invasive species can hurt the ecosystem because they have no natural enemies.

📈 Reading 3 — Populations & Carrying Capacity

SOL ENV.5 · ~25 minutes

A population is all the same kind of organism in one place. (Like all the deer in one forest.)

Populations grow when there is plenty of food, water, and space. They shrink when there isn't.

Carrying capacity

The carrying capacity of an area is the biggest population it can support. If there are too many animals, some will starve or move away.

Limiting factors

A limiting factor is anything that stops a population from growing. Common ones:

  • Food
  • Water
  • Space / shelter
  • Predators
  • Disease

Human population

The human population is now about 8 billion. It is still growing. This puts pressure on water, food, and natural resources.

⛏️ Reading 4 — Natural Resources & Energy

SOL ENV.6 · ~25 minutes

A natural resource is anything from nature that people use. There are two kinds:

  • Renewable — can be replaced fast (sunlight, wind, trees, water)
  • Non-renewable — cannot be replaced fast (oil, gas, coal, gold)

Fossil fuels

Fossil fuels = oil, gas, and coal. They come from dead plants and animals that lived millions of years ago. We burn them for energy. When they burn they release carbon dioxide (CO₂) into the air.

Renewable energy

  • Solar — sunlight
  • Wind — wind turbines
  • Hydro — moving water (rivers, dams)
  • Geothermal — heat from inside the Earth
  • Biomass — plants and waste
Virginia note: Virginia uses a mix of natural gas, nuclear, coal, solar, and wind. The state is building more solar farms and offshore wind every year.

🚯 Reading 5 — Pollution

SOL ENV.7 · ~25 minutes

Pollution is harmful stuff that gets into the air, water, or land. Almost all pollution comes from people.

Three kinds

  • Air pollution — smog, car exhaust, factory smoke. Causes asthma and breathing problems.
  • Water pollution — oil spills, trash, sewage, farm chemicals running into rivers.
  • Land pollution — landfills, plastic, chemical waste in the soil.

Acid rain

When factories burn coal, they release sulfur and nitrogen into the air. These mix with rain and make acid rain, which can kill fish and trees.

The 3 Rs

The best way to fight pollution is the 3 Rs:

  1. Reduce — use less stuff
  2. Reuse — use things again
  3. Recycle — turn old stuff into new stuff

The EPA

The Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) is the U.S. government office that protects the environment. They make rules about clean air, clean water, and dangerous chemicals.

🌡️ Reading 6 — Climate Change

SOL ENV.8 · ~25 minutes

Weather = what's happening outside today.

Climate = the average weather over many years.

The greenhouse effect

Some gases in the air trap heat from the Sun. This is the greenhouse effect. It is natural and good — without it, Earth would be too cold.

BUT — when we burn too many fossil fuels, we put extra CO₂ and other greenhouse gases in the air. They trap MORE heat. Earth gets warmer. This is global warming.

Effects of climate change

  • Polar ice melts → sea levels rise
  • Hotter summers, more wildfires
  • Stronger storms and hurricanes
  • Droughts in some places, floods in others
  • Animals lose their habitats (polar bears, coral reefs)
Virginia impact: Coastal cities like Norfolk and Virginia Beach are seeing more flooding because the ocean is rising. The Chesapeake Bay is getting warmer.

Solutions

  • Use renewable energy (solar, wind)
  • Drive less, use buses/trains/bikes
  • Plant trees
  • Use less electricity
  • Eat less meat (especially beef)

Economics & Personal Finance

5 short readings · 30-term vocab drill · 40-question EOC test · 1 budget project

💰 Section 1 — What is Economics?

Virginia SOL CE.11 · ~30 minutes

Economics is the study of how people make choices about money and things. People want a lot of things, but there is not enough of everything for everyone. This is called scarcity.

Because of scarcity, you have to choose. When you choose one thing, you give up another thing. The thing you give up is called the opportunity cost.

Example: You have $10. You can buy a movie ticket OR lunch. If you buy the movie ticket, the lunch is your opportunity cost. You gave up the lunch.

The three big questions every economy must answer

  • What should we make?
  • How should we make it?
  • Who gets it when it's made?

Different countries answer these questions in different ways. The United States uses a market economy. That means people and businesses make most of the choices — not the government.

🇺🇸 Section 2 — The U.S. Market Economy

Virginia SOL CE.12 · ~30 minutes

The United States uses something called the free enterprise system. That's a fancy way of saying:

  • People can choose what job they want.
  • People can own their stuff (this is called private property).
  • Businesses compete with each other to sell things.
  • People are free to start a business (this is called entrepreneurship).

Supply and Demand

Supply = how much of something there is to sell.

Demand = how much people want to buy it.

When demand is high and supply is low, the price goes up. When demand is low and supply is high, the price goes down.

Quick example: Concert tickets for Taylor Swift = high demand, low supply → very expensive. Last year's school yearbook = low demand, high supply → cheap or free.

Consumers and Producers

  • Consumers buy things. (You are a consumer when you buy lunch.)
  • Producers make and sell things. (Apple is a producer when it makes iPhones.)

🏛️ Section 3 — The Role of Government

Virginia SOL CE.13 · ~25 minutes

The government does NOT control most of the economy in the U.S. — but it does some important jobs:

  • Provides public goods — things everyone uses, like roads, parks, schools, and police.
  • Collects taxes — money from people and businesses to pay for public goods.
  • Makes regulations — rules to keep businesses fair (no cheating, no dangerous products).
  • Protects property rights — your stuff stays your stuff.

The Federal Reserve (the "Fed")

The Fed is the U.S. central bank. It controls how much money there is and how high interest rates are. When the economy is slow, the Fed lowers interest rates so people will borrow money and spend. When prices rise too fast (inflation), the Fed raises interest rates.

💼 Section 4 — Personal Finance & Careers

Virginia SOL CE.14 · ~45 minutes

Choosing a career

Three things matter when choosing a career:

  • Your talents — what you are good at.
  • Your interests — what you enjoy doing.
  • Job demand — what jobs are out there.

The skills employers want most are called work ethic skills: showing up on time, working hard, being honest, getting along with others, and finishing what you start.

Income, expenses, and budgeting

Income = money you earn (from a job).

Expenses = money you spend (rent, food, phone, fun).

A budget is a plan that says: "Here is my income. Here is where it will go."

Simple budget rule (50/30/20): 50% for needs (rent, food). 30% for wants (fun stuff). 20% for savings.

Saving and credit

  • Saving = putting money away for later. A savings account pays you a little extra (called interest).
  • Credit = borrowing money. A credit card lets you buy now and pay later. If you don't pay it back fast, you owe extra money (interest).
  • Debt = money you owe. Bad debt grows fast. Good debt (like a student loan) can help you earn more in the future.

Investing

Investing = using money to try to make more money. The most common is buying stocks (small pieces of a company). Stocks can go up OR down — there is risk.

🎯 Section 5 — Quick Recap

Before you move to Vocab Drill or the EOC Test, here are the 10 biggest ideas you should remember:

  1. Scarcity means we can't have everything.
  2. Opportunity cost is the thing you give up when you choose.
  3. The U.S. uses a free enterprise / market economy.
  4. Supply & demand sets prices.
  5. Consumers buy. Producers make & sell.
  6. Government provides public goods, collects taxes, makes regulations.
  7. The Fed controls interest rates and the money supply.
  8. Pick a career using your talents + interests + job demand.
  9. A budget is income minus expenses, with a plan for savings.
  10. Saving grows money. Debt grows fast if you don't pay it.

Cold War & Decolonization

WHII.10 + WHII.11 · Cold War · Korea · Vietnam · independence movements · 30-question final test

🌍 The World After WWII

SOL WHII.10 · ~20 min

World War II ended in 1945. The Allies won. Germany, Italy, and Japan were defeated. But the world that came out of the war was very different from the one before.

Two countries came out of WWII as superpowers — much more powerful than anyone else:

  • The United States (USA) — capitalist, democratic, free-market
  • The Soviet Union (USSR) — communist, single-party, government-controlled

These two powers had completely different ideas about how a country should work. And they soon stopped being allies.

Why "Cold" War? The USA and USSR never fought each other directly. If they had, it would have meant nuclear war. Instead, they competed everywhere else — spying, weapons, sports, space, and supporting opposite sides in other countries' wars. "Cold" means tense — but not actually shooting at each other.

Two big ideas in conflict

  • Capitalism (USA) — Private businesses. You own your own stuff. You vote.
  • Communism (USSR) — Government owns everything. One party rules. No real elections.

Two big alliances

  • NATO (1949) — the USA + Western Europe + Canada
  • Warsaw Pact (1955) — the USSR + Eastern Europe

🧊 The Cold War (1945–1991)

SOL WHII.10 · ~30 min

From the late 1940s to 1991, the USA and USSR were enemies. They never declared war, but they did everything else to win.

Key strategies

  • Containment — The USA's plan to stop communism from spreading.
  • Massive retaliation — Both sides built nuclear weapons. If you attack me, I will destroy you (and we will all die). Also called MAD — Mutual Assured Destruction.
  • Domino theory — The USA thought if ONE country became communist, others nearby would fall too — like dominoes.
  • Proxy wars — Wars where the USA and USSR did not fight directly, but each supported a different side.

Timeline of major events

1947
Truman Doctrine
USA promises to help any country resisting communism. Beginning of "containment."
1947–1951
Marshall Plan
USA sends billions to rebuild Western Europe after WWII — partly to keep them from going communist.
1948–1949
Berlin Blockade & Airlift
USSR cuts off West Berlin. USA flies in food & supplies by plane for almost a year.
1949
NATO formed
USA + Western Europe military alliance.
1949
China becomes communist
Mao Zedong wins China's civil war. The biggest country in Asia is now communist. USA panics.
1950–1953
Korean War
First "hot" war of the Cold War. USA fights for South Korea; USSR + China back the North.
1955
Warsaw Pact
USSR + Eastern Europe military alliance — response to NATO.
1961
Berlin Wall built
USSR builds a wall to stop East Germans from escaping to West Berlin.
1962
Cuban Missile Crisis
USSR puts nuclear missiles in Cuba — 90 miles from Florida. 13 days the world held its breath. War almost happened.
1955–1975
Vietnam War
Another proxy war. USA backs South Vietnam, USSR + China back the communist North. USA loses.
1989
Berlin Wall falls
Communist governments in Eastern Europe collapse one after another.
1991
USSR collapses
The Soviet Union breaks apart into 15 separate countries. Cold War ends. USA wins.
Why did the USSR collapse? The Soviet economy got weaker over the years. People wanted more freedom and better food. Spending money on the arms race and the Afghanistan War (1979–1989) drained them. Mikhail Gorbachev's reforms (glasnost = openness, perestroika = restructuring) opened the door — and the whole system fell apart.

🪖 Korea & Vietnam — The Hot Wars of the Cold War

SOL WHII.10 · ~30 min

The Korean War (1950–1953)

After WWII, Korea was split at the 38th parallel (a line on the map):

  • North Korea — communist, supported by USSR & China
  • South Korea — non-communist, supported by USA

In 1950, North Korea invaded South Korea. The United Nations (led by the USA) sent troops to push the North back. China then joined in to help the North.

The war went back and forth for 3 years. By 1953 there was a cease-fire (not a peace treaty — they technically are still at war!) at the same 38th parallel where it started.

Result: The two Koreas are still split today. North Korea is one of the most isolated and poor countries. South Korea is a rich democracy that makes Samsung phones and K-pop.

The Vietnam War (1955–1975)

Vietnam had been a colony of France. After WWII, a communist leader named Ho Chi Minh wanted independence. France fought him and lost. Vietnam was then split:

  • North Vietnam — communist, led by Ho Chi Minh
  • South Vietnam — non-communist, backed by USA

The USA got more and more involved through the 1960s. Why? The Domino Theory. If Vietnam fell to communism, all of Southeast Asia might fall too.

At the war's peak, over 500,000 American soldiers were in Vietnam. The war was very unpopular at home in the USA. Many young Americans protested.

The USA pulled out in 1973. In 1975, North Vietnamese tanks rolled into Saigon (the South's capital) and won the war.

Why did the USA lose?
  • They were fighting a guerrilla war (hit-and-run) in a country they didn't understand.
  • The South Vietnamese government was corrupt and weak.
  • The American public lost support.
  • The communist North was patient — they were fighting for their homeland; the USA was 8,000 miles away.

Other proxy battlegrounds

The Cold War touched almost everywhere:

  • Cuba (1959) — Fidel Castro takes over and becomes communist. The USA tries (and fails) to invade in the Bay of Pigs.
  • Afghanistan (1979) — USSR invades. USA secretly arms the Afghan fighters. The USSR loses.
  • Latin America — civil wars in Nicaragua, El Salvador, Guatemala. USA backs anti-communist sides.
  • Africa — civil wars in Angola, Ethiopia, Mozambique. Both sides backed.

✊ Independence & Decolonization

SOL WHII.11 · ~25 min

🌿
⭐ Featured Activity
Davis and the Dispatches
An interactive choose-your-path game. Travel with 9th-grader Davis through India, South Africa, Vietnam, Egypt, and Ghana and make decisions about decolonization. Counts as a full Decolonization activity (about 45–60 minutes).
▶ Play Now →

Decolonization = when colonized countries became independent.

After WWII, the European empires were broke and exhausted. Most of Asia and Africa had been ruled by Britain, France, Belgium, the Netherlands, or Portugal. One by one, these colonies became independent in the 1940s, 50s, and 60s.

Key leaders

India · 1947
Mahatma Gandhi
Led India to independence from Britain using nonviolent protest. He inspired civil rights movements all over the world. After independence, India and Pakistan split apart.
Ghana · 1957
Kwame Nkrumah
Led Ghana to be the first sub-Saharan African country to become independent from European rule.
Kenya · 1963
Jomo Kenyatta
Led Kenya to independence from Britain after years of armed struggle (Mau Mau Uprising).
South Africa · 1994
Nelson Mandela
Spent 27 years in prison for fighting apartheid (a system that gave only white people rights). Released in 1990. Became the first Black president of South Africa.
Egypt · 1956
Gamal Abdel Nasser
Took control of the Suez Canal from Britain & France. A symbol of Arab independence.
Israel · 1948
Golda Meir
Helped create the modern state of Israel. Later became Prime Minister.

Common patterns

  • Many former colonies became poor after independence — Europe had taken resources for decades.
  • Borders drawn by Europeans often cut across tribal and ethnic groups, causing later conflict.
  • Both the USA and USSR tried to win over the new countries to their side. This pulled decolonization into the Cold War.
  • Some new countries became non-aligned — they picked neither side.
India and Pakistan: When the British left India in 1947, the country split into two — mostly Hindu India and mostly Muslim Pakistan. Over 1 million people died in the violence of partition. The two countries are still rivals today.

✊ The Civil Rights Movement (1950s–1960s)

SOL VUS.13 · ~30 min

After the Civil War (1861–1865) and the end of slavery, Black Americans were still treated unfairly — especially in the South. The system was called Jim Crow.

Black people could not vote freely. They had to go to separate schools, sit in the back of buses, and use separate water fountains. The schools and facilities for Black people were almost always worse.

In the 1950s and 1960s, Black Americans (joined by many white allies) organized a huge movement to change this. It is called the Civil Rights Movement.

Key events

1954
Brown v. Board of Education
The Supreme Court ruled that separate schools for Black and white children are unconstitutional. The famous line: "separate is not equal."
1955–1956
Montgomery Bus Boycott
Rosa Parks refused to give up her seat to a white man. Black community refused to ride city buses for over a year. Martin Luther King Jr. became a leader.
1960
Greensboro Sit-ins
Four Black college students sat at a 'white-only' lunch counter in North Carolina. The idea spread to dozens of cities.
1963
March on Washington
Over 250,000 people gathered. Martin Luther King Jr. gave his famous "I Have a Dream" speech.
1964
Civil Rights Act of 1964
President Lyndon B. Johnson signed it. Made it illegal to discriminate based on race in jobs, schools, restaurants, and other public places.
1965
Voting Rights Act of 1965
Made it illegal to use tricks (like 'literacy tests') to stop Black people from voting. Massive jump in Black voter registration in the South.
1968
MLK Assassinated
Dr. King was shot and killed in Memphis, Tennessee. He was only 39 years old. He became one of the most famous Americans in history.

Key leaders

  • Martin Luther King Jr. — main leader, used non-violent protest, modeled after Gandhi
  • Rosa Parks — refused to give up her bus seat in Montgomery
  • Malcolm X — argued for stronger action and Black self-defense
  • Thurgood Marshall — the lawyer who won Brown v. Board; later the first Black Supreme Court justice
  • President Lyndon B. Johnson — signed both Civil Rights and Voting Rights Acts

Virginia connections

Virginia was a key state in the Civil Rights story. The state government tried to "Massive Resistance" — closing public schools rather than letting Black and white children attend together. Prince Edward County in Virginia closed its schools for 5 years!

Today Virginia has come a long way: the state has elected Black governors, mayors, and senators.

🛣️ Modern America (1970s → Today)

SOL VUS.14–15 · ~25 min

After the Civil Rights Movement, America kept changing. Here are the big events of the last 50 years.

The 1970s — Trouble at home

  • Vietnam War ends (1975) — USA loses. Many Americans had protested the war.
  • Watergate scandal — President Nixon broke the law and lied about it. He resigned in 1974. Trust in government dropped.
  • Energy crisis — Long gas lines, high prices.

The 1980s — Reagan years & end of Cold War

  • Ronald Reagan was president (1981–1989). Cut taxes, increased military spending, talked tough to the USSR.
  • Computers started appearing in homes.
  • 1989 — Berlin Wall falls. Cold War ends.

The 1990s — The Internet age begins

  • 1991 — USSR breaks apart. The USA is the only superpower.
  • 1991 — Gulf War (USA pushed Iraq out of Kuwait).
  • Internet goes from a few computers to the whole world.
  • Economy is strong, jobs are easy to get.

The 2000s — Terrorism & war

  • September 11, 2001 — terrorists fly planes into the World Trade Center (NYC) and the Pentagon. Almost 3,000 people die. The world changed.
  • War in Afghanistan (2001–2021) — USA invades to stop al-Qaeda.
  • War in Iraq (2003–2011) — USA invades, removes Saddam Hussein.
  • 2008 — Big Great Recession hits — banks fail, many lose homes and jobs.

The 2010s and 2020s — A more diverse America

  • 2008 — Barack Obama elected — first Black president of the USA.
  • 2010s — Smartphones, social media change daily life.
  • 2015 — Same-sex marriage legal nationwide.
  • 2020 — COVID-19 pandemic kills over 1 million Americans.
  • 2020s — Climate change, AI, immigration, political division become big topics.
Virginia today: Once the capital of the Confederacy, Virginia today is one of America's most diverse states. Northern Virginia near DC is now home to people from every continent on Earth.

💭 Big Themes in US History

Use these for your writing project!

1. Freedom & Liberty

The USA was founded on the idea that people are born with rights. "Life, liberty, and the pursuit of happiness."

2. Equality (and the struggle for it)

The Constitution said "all men are created equal" in 1776 — but not everyone was actually treated equally. The whole story of US history is the long fight to make that promise real for everyone: Black Americans, women, immigrants, Native Americans, LGBT people.

3. Immigration & the "Melting Pot"

The USA is a country of immigrants. Wave after wave came — from Europe, Asia, Africa, Latin America. Each wave faced discrimination at first. Each wave also changed America.

4. Democracy

People choose their leaders by voting. Power is split between branches of government. Even the President is not above the law.

5. Change Through Protest

Almost every big change in US history came from people protesting — workers, women, Black Americans, anti-war activists. Peaceful protest is part of the American DNA.

6. Hard Work & Opportunity

The "American Dream" — the idea that if you work hard, you can have a better life than your parents — has pulled millions of people to America from around the world.
